steps.title: Import React and useState from 'react'
steps.instruction: Import React and the useState hook from the 'react' package.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in React and useState from the 'react' module.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of importing React and useState
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.seedCode: // Import React and useState from 'react' here
steps.expectedOutcome: The React library and useState hook are imported, making them available for use in the component.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported React and useState. This gives you access to React's core functionality and the useState hook for state management.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check your import syntax. Make sure you're importing both React and useState from the 'react' package.
steps.feedbackWrong: That doesn't look right. You need to import React and useState from the 'react' package using the import statement.

steps.title: Create the useFetch component function
steps.instruction: Create a function called useFetch that accepts a generic type parameter T. The function should return a JSX.Element (or React.ReactElement).
steps.hint: Start by writing 'function useFetch<T>()' or 'const useFetch = <T,>() =>'. Remember to include the generic parameter T.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';

// Create the useFetch function with generic type parameter T here
steps.expectedOutcome: A function named useFetch is defined with a generic type parameter T.
successCriteria: Generic type parameter T is declared
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the useFetch function with a generic type parameter T.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you've created a function named useFetch that accepts a generic type parameter T and returns JSX.Element.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function isn't quite right. Remember to create a function called useFetch with a generic type parameter T.

steps.title: Add URL parameter to useFetch
steps.instruction: Add a parameter named 'url' to the useFetch function. The parameter should be typed as 'string'.
steps.hint: Add the parameter inside the parentheses after the generic type parameter T. Remember to include the type annotation.
steps.expectedOutcome: The useFetch function should accept a 'url' parameter with the correct TypeScript string type.
successCriteria: The useFetch function has a parameter named 'url' with type annotation ': string'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added the URL parameter with proper TypeScript typing. This allows the hook to know which endpoint to fetch data from.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you've added a parameter named 'url' and given it the correct type annotation ': string'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The URL parameter is missing or incorrectly typed. Remember to add 'url: string' as a parameter to the useFetch function.

steps.title: Define the return type interface
steps.instruction: Inside your useFetch function, define a TypeScript interface called FetchResult<T> with three properties: data of type T | null, loading of type boolean, and error of type string | null.
steps.hint: Use the 'interface' keyword followed by the interface name and generic type parameter <T>. Define each property with its type annotation.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a properly typed interface that describes what your hook will return.
successCriteria: The code must include an interface named FetchResult with generic type parameter <T>, containing data: T | null, loading: boolean, and error: string | null properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully defined the FetchResult<T> interface with the correct properties and types. This will give us type safety for the hook's return value.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that your interface has all three required properties with the correct TypeScript types: data should be T | null, loading should be boolean, and error should be string | null.
steps.feedbackWrong: The interface definition is missing or incorrect. Remember to use the 'interface' keyword, name it FetchResult<T>, and include all three properties with their proper TypeScript type annotations.

steps.title: Initialize state for data
steps.instruction: Inside your useFetch function, use useState to create a state variable named 'data' initialized to null, with the type T | null.
steps.hint: Use the useState hook you imported earlier. Remember to specify the generic type parameter for useState as T | null.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of typed state initialization
const [data, setData] = useState<T | null>(null);
steps.expectedOutcome: The useFetch function will have a properly typed data state variable initialized to null.
successCriteria: The code should include a useState call with generic type T | null, initialized to null, and the variable should be named 'data'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully initialized the data state with the correct type T | null.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're using useState with the generic type T | null and initializing it to null.
steps.feedbackWrong: That doesn't match what we need. We need to create a state variable named 'data' with type T | null, initialized to null using useState.

steps.title: Initialize state for loading
steps.instruction: Inside your useFetch function, use the useState hook to create a state variable named 'loading' initialized to true, with the type boolean.
steps.hint: Call useState<boolean>(true) and destructure the array to get the loading state and its setter.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of initializing a boolean loading state
const [loading, setLoading] = useState<boolean>(true);
steps.expectedOutcome: The useFetch function now has a loading state variable initialized to true.
successCriteria: The code includes a useState call for loading with type boolean and initial value true.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added the loading state to track when data is being fetched.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that loading is typed as boolean and initialized to true.
steps.feedbackWrong: The loading state initialization is missing or incorrect. Use useState<boolean>(true) to create it.

steps.title: Initialize state for error
steps.instruction: Initialize a state variable named 'error' using useState, typed as 'string | null' and initialized to null.
steps.hint: Use the useState hook with the generic type parameter <string | null> and pass null as the initial value.
steps.expectedOutcome: The error state is declared and ready to store any error messages that occur during fetching.
successCriteria: The code includes a useState call for 'error' with type 'string | null' and initial value null.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully initialized the error state. This will allow your hook to track and report any errors that occur during data fetching.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you've declared 'error' with useState, typed it as 'string | null', and initialized it to null.
steps.feedbackWrong: The error state initialization is missing or incorrect. Please use useState to create an 'error' state variable with type 'string | null' and initial value null.

steps.title: Create the fetchData function
steps.instruction: Inside your useFetch function, create an async function named fetchData that doesn't take any parameters.
steps.hint: Use the async keyword before the function definition. The function should be declared inside the hook but before the return statement.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have an async function named fetchData declared inside your useFetch hook.
successCriteria: The code must include an async function named fetchData defined inside the useFetch function body.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the fetchData function. This will be the core function that performs the API request.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you've created an async function named fetchData inside the useFetch hook.
steps.feedbackWrong: The fetchData function wasn't created correctly. Remember to declare an async function named fetchData inside your useFetch hook.

steps.title: Implement the fetch logic in fetchData
steps.instruction: Inside the fetchData function, implement the fetch logic to get data from the URL parameter. Use the fetch API with async/await, handle the response, and update the data, loading, and error states appropriately.
steps.hint: Remember to set loading to true before fetching, handle both success and error cases, and update all three state variables (data, loading, error) accordingly.
steps.expectedOutcome: The fetchData function will contain the complete fetch implementation with proper error handling and state updates.
successCriteria: The fetchData function should: 1) Set loading to true at the start, 2) Use fetch with the url parameter, 3) Handle both successful and failed responses, 4) Update data, loading, and error states appropriately.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully implemented the fetch logic with proper error handling and state management.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check if you're: 1) Setting loading to true before fetching, 2) Handling both success and error cases, 3) Updating all three state variables (data, loading, error).
steps.feedbackWrong: The fetchData function doesn't seem to have the complete fetch implementation. Review the example and make sure you're using the fetch API with async/await and updating all state variables.

steps.title: Call fetchData with useEffect
steps.instruction: Import useEffect from 'react' and add a useEffect hook inside your useFetch function that calls fetchData when the url parameter changes.
steps.hint: Add the useEffect import, then implement useEffect with fetchData as the effect and [url] as the dependency array.
steps.expectedOutcome: The useFetch hook will automatically fetch data when the URL changes by using the useEffect hook.
successCriteria: The code should import useEffect from 'react' and add a useEffect hook that calls fetchData with [url] as the dependency array.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added the useEffect hook to trigger data fetching when the URL changes. This ensures your hook automatically fetches new data whenever the URL parameter updates.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've both imported useEffect and implemented it correctly. The useEffect should call fetchData and have [url] as its dependency array.
steps.feedbackWrong: The useEffect hook wasn't properly added. Remember to import useEffect from 'react' and add it inside your useFetch function to call fetchData when the url changes.

steps.title: Return the FetchResult object
steps.instruction: Return an object with data, loading, and error properties from the useFetch hook, matching the FetchResult<T> interface structure.
steps.hint: At the end of your hook, return an object containing the three state variables you've already defined.
steps.expectedOutcome: The useFetch hook now returns an object with data, loading, and error properties that match the FetchResult<T> interface.
successCriteria: The hook should return an object containing the three state variables: data, loading, and error.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully returned the state values from your custom hook. The hook now provides all the necessary data to components that use it.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're returning an object with exactly three properties: data, loading, and error. Check that you're using the correct variable names.
steps.feedbackWrong: The hook should return an object containing the three state variables. Look at the state variables you've defined earlier in the hook and return them as an object.

steps.title: Add TypeScript return type annotation
steps.instruction: Add a return type annotation to the useFetch function signature. The function should explicitly declare that it returns FetchResult<T>.
steps.hint: After the parameter list and before the opening curly brace, add a colon followed by the interface name you defined earlier.
steps.expectedOutcome: The useFetch function signature will include a proper TypeScript return type annotation, making the function's return type explicit and type-safe.
successCriteria: The useFetch function signature includes a colon after the parameter list
The return type is specified as FetchResult<T>
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've added the return type annotation to make the function's contract explicit. This completes your generic useFetch<T> hook implementation.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but the return type annotation needs to be exactly FetchResult<T> after the colon. Check the interface name and generic parameter.
steps.feedbackWrong: The return type annotation is missing or incorrect. Remember to add ': FetchResult<T>' after the parameter list in the function signature.
